summary: A crested, thick-billed songbird whose scarlet males are the most familiar red bird of eastern North America. Unusually among North American songbirds, females sing too, sometimes from the nest itself, and pairs stay together year-round.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America from southern Canada through the eastern US to Mexico, Belize and northern Guatemala; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Both sexes sing; female song often signals the male to bring food to the nest
Heavy conical bill cracks hard seeds such as sunflower and safflower
Has expanded its range far northward over the past century, helped by bird feeders and suburban shrubbery
Red plumage comes from carotenoid pigments in its diet

animal.diet: Seeds, fruit and insects; nestlings fed mostly insects
animal.habitat: Thickets, woodland edges, hedgerows, suburban gardens and desert washes
animal.lifespan: Usually under 3 years in the wild; banding record about 15 years
animal.behaviour: Territorial males (and sometimes females) attack their own reflections in windows and car mirrors in spring, sometimes for hours.
fieldMarks: Male entirely red with a black face mask around a thick red-orange bill
Prominent pointed crest in both sexes
Female warm buff-brown with reddish tinges on crest, wings and tail
Long tail; juveniles have a dark bill
animal.voice: Loud, clear, slurred whistles repeated in series, often rendered 'cheer-cheer-cheer' or 'birdie-birdie-birdie'; call a sharp metallic 'chip'.
animal.lookalikes: Pyrrhuloxia (south-western US and Mexico) is grey with a red crest and a stubby yellow bill. Summer Tanager males are all red but lack the crest and black face. Scarlet Tanager has black wings.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any eastern US backyard feeder, park or thicket; common through the south-east and Mississippi Valley.

lore: Named after the red robes of Roman Catholic cardinals, it is the official state bird of seven US states — Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, Virginia and West Virginia — more than any other species.
funFact: Linnaeus first named it Loxia cardinalis in 1758, putting it in the same genus as crossbills.

summary: North America's most widespread thrush, a red-breasted lawn hunter whose caroling is often the first song heard before dawn. English colonists named it after the unrelated European robin because of its orange breast.
nativeRange: Breeds from Alaska and Canada to southern Mexico; northern birds winter south to the Gulf coast, Mexico and Guatemala
abilities: Hunts earthworms by running, stopping and cocking its head, locating prey largely by sight
Shifts from a mainly worm and insect diet in summer to fruit and berries in winter
Builds a cup nest with a mud lining, shaped by the female pressing with her breast
Lays the sky-blue eggs that gave the name 'robin's egg blue'

animal.diet: Earthworms, insect larvae, and fruit such as holly, juniper and crabapple
animal.habitat: Lawns, parks, open woodland, farmland and forest to the tree line
animal.lifespan: About 2 years on average; banding record nearly 14 years
animal.behaviour: In winter many robins form large nomadic flocks that follow fruit crops and roost communally, often unnoticed because they stop singing on lawns.
fieldMarks: Brick-orange breast and belly contrasting with grey-brown back
Blackish head with broken white eye-ring
Yellow bill; white lower belly and undertail
Juveniles have heavily spotted breasts, showing the thrush family resemblance
animal.voice: A rich, caroling series of whistled phrases, often rendered 'cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio'; calls include a sharp 'tut-tut' and a high thin 'seee' alarm for hawks.
animal.lookalikes: Varied Thrush (west) has an orange eyebrow, orange wing bars and a black breast band. Eastern Towhee has rufous only on the flanks with a white belly. Spotted juveniles may suggest other thrushes but already show some orange.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, parks and gardens throughout the US and Canada; winter flocks in fruiting trees across the southern states.
animal.season: Resident across much of the US; summer visitor in Canada and Alaska, Mar–Oct

lore: It is the state bird of Connecticut, Michigan and Wisconsin, and its spring return has long been treated across North America as a sign that winter is ending.
funFact: Many American robins never leave the northern states in winter; they simply switch to fruit and become quiet, so their 'first of spring' sightings are often birds that were there all along.

summary: A loud, crested corvid of eastern North America, brilliant blue above and white below. It caches thousands of acorns each autumn, and the ones it forgets are credited with helping oak forests spread north after the Ice Age.
nativeRange: Southern Canada and the eastern and central United States, west to the Rockies' foothills
abilities: Carries several acorns at once in an expandable throat pouch and buries them far from the parent tree
Mimics the screams of Red-shouldered and Red-tailed Hawks
Blue colour is structural — feathers scatter light; there is no blue pigment
Mobs owls and hawks in noisy groups

animal.diet: Acorns, beechnuts, seeds, insects; occasionally eggs and nestlings
animal.habitat: Oak and beech forest, mixed woodland, suburbs and parks
animal.lifespan: Typically about 7 years; banding record over 26 years
animal.behaviour: Some populations migrate in loose daytime flocks along lakeshores and coasts in autumn, but which individuals migrate varies from year to year and is not well understood.
fieldMarks: Bright blue crest, back, wings and tail
Black necklace across whitish throat and face
Bold white wing bars and white tail corners, black barring on wings and tail
Crest raised when excited, flattened when calm
animal.voice: A harsh, screaming 'jay! jay!'; also a musical, squeaky 'queedle-queedle' (the 'pump-handle' call), soft clicks, and convincing hawk imitations.
animal.lookalikes: Steller's Jay (west) has a black front half and no white in the wings or tail. Florida Scrub-Jay lacks a crest and white spots. Belted Kingfisher is blue-grey with a huge bill and a ragged crest.
animal.whereToSee: Oak woods, parks and feeders offering peanuts across the eastern US; migrating flocks along the Great Lakes shores (e.g. Whitefish Point, Michigan) in September.
animal.season: Resident; some northern birds migrate Sep–Oct and Apr–May

lore: Mark Catesby illustrated it as 'The Blew Jay' in his Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands (1731–43); it is now the emblem of Toronto's Major League Baseball team.
funFact: A single blue jay may cache an estimated 3,000–5,000 acorns in one autumn.

summary: A flame-orange and black blackbird relative that weaves a hanging, sock-like nest high in the outer branches of elms and maples. It winters in the tropics, where it sips nectar and eats fruit.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern and central North America; winters from southern Mexico to Colombia and Venezuela, with some in Florida and the Caribbean
abilities: Weaves a pendant pouch nest from plant fibres, hair and string, hung from slender twig tips
Uses 'gaping' — stabbing the closed bill into fruit and prying it open — to drink juice
Visits flowers for nectar on the wintering grounds, carrying pollen between blooms
Migrates by night between the US and northern South America

animal.diet: Caterpillars and other insects, ripe fruit, nectar
animal.habitat: Open deciduous woodland, riversides, parks with tall shade trees
animal.behaviour: Readily comes to feeders offering orange halves and grape jelly during spring migration.
fieldMarks: Adult male: fiery orange underparts, rump and tail sides; entirely black head and back
Black wings with a single white wing bar
Female and first-year male: yellow-orange below, olive-brown above, two white wing bars
Sharply pointed, straight grey bill
animal.voice: Rich, flute-like whistled phrases, varying from bird to bird; call a dry, chattering rattle.
animal.lookalikes: Bullock's Oriole (west) has an orange face with a black eye-line and a large white wing patch; the two hybridise on the Great Plains. Orchard Oriole males are deep chestnut, not orange. American Redstart is a tiny warbler with orange tail patches.
animal.whereToSee: Shade trees along rivers and in older parks across the eastern US and southern Canada; migration hotspots such as Magee Marsh (Ohio) and Point Pelee (Ontario) in May.

lore: Its orange and black recalled the heraldic colours of the Calverts, the Lords Baltimore who founded colonial Maryland; it is now Maryland's state bird and the namesake of Baltimore's baseball team.
funFact: Before Dutch elm disease, the American elm was its classic nesting tree; orioles have since shifted to maples, cottonwoods and sycamores.

summary: A plump, cinnamon-backed thrush of eastern forests with bold black spots on a white breast. Its flute-like song is one of the most celebrated sounds in North American nature, produced partly by singing two notes at once.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern North America; winters from southern Mexico to Panama
abilities: Its two-sided syrinx lets it sound two independent notes simultaneously, harmonising with itself
Migrates at night across or around the Gulf of Mexico
Forages by flicking through leaf litter for invertebrates
Relies on calcium-rich prey such as snails when laying eggs

animal.diet: Leaf-litter insects, spiders, snails and earthworms; fruit before migration
animal.habitat: Moist, mature deciduous and mixed forest with a shrubby understorey
animal.behaviour: It often adds white material — paper, plastic or birch bark — to the base of its nest.
fieldMarks: Bright cinnamon-rufous upperparts, brightest on the crown and nape
White underparts with large, round black spots
Bold white eye-ring
Plump, short-tailed thrush shape
animal.voice: A three-part song: soft introductory notes, a liquid flute-like 'ee-oh-lay', then a trilled, buzzy flourish that may contain two notes at once; call a rapid 'pit-pit-pit'.
animal.lookalikes: Hermit Thrush has a rufous tail contrasting with a browner back and smaller spots. Veery has only faint spotting. Brown Thrasher has a long tail, yellow eyes, wing bars and streaks rather than round spots.
animal.whereToSee: Shady deciduous forest across the eastern US — e.g. Great Smoky Mountains, Shenandoah, Rock Creek Park in Washington DC; dusk is the best time to hear it.

lore: Henry David Thoreau praised its song repeatedly in his journals as the finest of any bird, and it has been the official bird of the District of Columbia since 1938.
funFact: Breeding Bird Survey counts show the wood thrush has declined by roughly half since the 1960s, largely through forest fragmentation and wintering-habitat loss.

summary: A tiny, fearless black-capped tit that survives northern winters in a body weighing about 11 g. Its namesake call works as a code: the more 'dee' notes, the more dangerous the predator.
nativeRange: Alaska, Canada and the northern half of the United States
abilities: Adds extra 'dee' notes to its alarm call for smaller, more dangerous predators such as pygmy-owls
Caches thousands of seeds each autumn and remembers their locations
Its hippocampus — the brain region for spatial memory — gains new neurons in autumn, when caching peaks
Lowers its body temperature by about 10 °C on cold nights to save energy (regulated hypothermia)

animal.diet: Insects, spiders and eggs in summer; seeds and berries in winter
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodland, willow thickets, parks and gardens
animal.lifespan: Usually 2–3 years; banding record about 11 years
animal.behaviour: In winter it forms the core of mixed-species flocks that nuthatches, kinglets and woodpeckers join for safety.
fieldMarks: Black cap and black bib separated by bright white cheeks
Grey back; buffy flanks
White edges to wing coverts and secondaries form a pale wing panel
Tiny bill; large-headed, round-bodied shape
animal.voice: The familiar 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee'; song a clear, two-note whistle 'fee-bee', the second note lower.
animal.lookalikes: Carolina Chickadee (south-east) is smaller, shows less white in the wing and sings a four-note 'fee-bee-fee-bay'; the two hybridise where ranges meet. Mountain Chickadee has a white eyebrow; Boreal Chickadee has a brown cap.
animal.whereToSee: Any feeder or woodland in the northern US and Canada; very tame birds take seed from the hand at many nature centres.

lore: It is the state bird of Maine and Massachusetts and the provincial bird of New Brunswick.
funFact: Chickadees of other species and even nuthatches respond to black-capped chickadee alarm calls, effectively eavesdropping on its predator warnings.

summary: A sleek, crested fruit-eater with a black mask and red wax-like droplets on its wing tips. It roams in tight, whistling flocks wherever berries ripen, and can live on fruit alone for months.
nativeRange: Breeds across southern Canada and the northern US; winters throughout most of the US south to Central America and the Caribbean
abilities: Can survive on fruit alone for months, digesting it rapidly
Disperses seeds of cedar, juniper, serviceberry and many other fruiting plants
Flocks pass berries from bird to bird along a branch
Sallies out over rivers in summer to catch flying insects

animal.diet: Berries and small fruits; flying insects in summer
animal.habitat: Open woodland, forest edges, orchards and suburbs with fruiting trees
animal.behaviour: It nests late in summer, timed to fruit ripening, and can become intoxicated or die from eating fermented berries.
fieldMarks: Silky, warm brown-grey plumage with a pointed crest
Narrow black mask edged with white
Yellow belly and yellow-tipped tail
Red waxy tips on the secondary feathers
animal.voice: No true song; very high, thin, buzzy whistles 'sreee' given constantly by flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Bohemian Waxwing is larger and greyer, with rufous undertail coverts and yellow and white marks on the wings. Northern Cardinal females share the crest but have a thick red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Fruiting trees anywhere in North America, especially junipers, crabapples and mountain-ash in winter; along rivers catching insects in summer.
animal.season: Present year-round in much of the north-central US; nomadic, with numbers changing with fruit crops

lore: Mark Catesby painted it in the 1730s as 'The Chatterer', and its sociable habits earned it the old American names 'cedar-bird' and 'cherry-bird'.
funFact: Since the 1960s, some cedar waxwings have orange instead of yellow tail tips — the result of eating berries of introduced Morrow's honeysuckle while their feathers grow.

summary: A slim grey bird with a big voice, famous for copying the songs of other birds, frogs and even car alarms. Males may learn around 200 different songs, repeating each phrase several times before switching.
nativeRange: Southern Canada and the US south to southern Mexico, the Bahamas and the Greater Antilles; introduced to Hawaii and Bermuda
abilities: Learns new song types throughout life, adding mimicry of birds, frogs, insects and mechanical sounds
Unmated males sing through the night, especially under bright moonlight or streetlights
Recognises individual humans who have approached its nest and scolds them on sight
Flashes white wing patches while foraging, possibly to startle insects

animal.diet: Insects in summer; fruit and berries in autumn and winter
animal.habitat: Open ground with shrubs and trees — suburbs, hedgerows, parks, desert edges
animal.behaviour: It aggressively defends nests and winter fruit trees, diving at cats, hawks and people.
fieldMarks: Grey above, paler grey-white below
Large white patches on dark wings, obvious in flight
Long dark tail with white outer feathers
Thin, slightly decurved dark bill; yellow eye in adults
animal.voice: Long, varied runs of phrases, each repeated three or more times in a row, mixing its own song with mimicry; call a harsh 'chack'.
animal.lookalikes: Loggerhead Shrike has a black mask and a hooked bill and flies with fast, low wingbeats. Gray Catbird is dark slate with a black cap and rusty undertail. Townsend's Solitaire (west) has an eye-ring and buffy wing patches.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, parking-lot shrubs and fence posts throughout the southern US; abundant in Texas and Florida.
animal.season: Resident; northernmost birds partly withdraw in winter

lore: Thomas Jefferson kept a pet mockingbird named Dick at the President's House, and the species gave Harper Lee the title of To Kill a Mockingbird (1960); it is the state bird of Arkansas, Florida, Mississippi, Tennessee and Texas.
funFact: Its scientific name means 'many-tongued mimic', and its Nahuatl-derived Spanish name cenzontle means 'four hundred voices'.

summary: The male is perhaps the most colourful songbird in North America — blue head, red underparts and a lime-green back. Females are the only bright green finch-like bird in their range, and the species was long trapped as a cage bird.
nativeRange: Breeds in two separate populations — the south-eastern Atlantic coast (North Carolina to Florida) and the south-central US and northern Mexico; winters in Florida, the Bahamas, Cuba, Mexico and Central America to Panama
abilities: Western birds pause in the south-western US and north-western Mexico to moult before finishing migration — an unusual 'moult migration'
Males do not reach full colour until their second autumn; first-year males look like females
Males fight fiercely over territories, sometimes drawing blood

animal.diet: Grass and weed seeds; insects in the breeding season
animal.habitat: Brushy thickets, woodland edges, maritime scrub and overgrown fields
animal.behaviour: Despite the male's colours, it is secretive and sings from within cover more often than from open perches.
fieldMarks: Adult male: deep blue head, red eye-ring, red underparts and rump, yellow-green back
Female and immature: bright, uniform yellowish-green with a pale eye-ring
Short conical bill typical of buntings
Small, compact size
animal.voice: A sweet, high, run-on warble of musical notes; call a soft 'chip'.
animal.lookalikes: Female Indigo Bunting is brown, not green. Varied Bunting males are dark purple with a red nape. Green female could suggest a vireo or warbler, but the stubby conical bill identifies it.
animal.whereToSee: Coastal thickets of South Carolina, Georgia and north-east Florida; Texas Hill Country; feeders in south Florida in winter.
animal.season: Summer visitor in the US, Apr–Sep; winters in Florida and the tropics

lore: Mark Catesby painted it as 'The Painted Finch' in the 1730s, and it was exported to Europe as a cage bird; in the Caribbean and Mexico trapping for the pet trade continues to threaten it.
funFact: Its French name nonpareil means 'without equal'.

summary: A blazing red bird with jet-black wings that sings unseen high in the canopy of eastern forests. After breeding the male turns yellow-green, keeping only his black wings, before flying to the Andes for the winter.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern North America; winters in north-western South America, mainly along the eastern Andean foothills from Colombia to Bolivia
abilities: Undergoes a complete colour change: scarlet in summer, olive-yellow in autumn and winter
Migrates thousands of kilometres between the US and South America
Gleans caterpillars from the high canopy, controlling forest insect pests

animal.diet: Caterpillars, beetles and other canopy insects; fruit in autumn
animal.habitat: Large tracts of mature deciduous and oak–hickory forest
animal.behaviour: It is sensitive to forest fragmentation and is scarce or absent in small woodlots.
fieldMarks: Breeding male: brilliant scarlet body with solid black wings and tail
Female and winter male: olive-green above, yellow below, with dark wings
No wing bars
Stout, pale, rather blunt bill
animal.voice: A hoarse, burry series of phrases, often described as 'a robin with a sore throat'; call a distinctive 'chick-burr'.
animal.lookalikes: Summer Tanager male is entirely rose-red including the wings. Northern Cardinal has a crest and a black face. Western Tanager has wing bars; female orioles have pointed bills and wing bars.
animal.whereToSee: Mature oak forests of the eastern US, e.g. the Appalachians; on migration at sites such as Magee Marsh (Ohio) and Central Park (New York) in May.

funFact: Its species name olivacea ('olive-green') describes the plumage of females and young birds, not the scarlet breeding male.

summary: A small thrush of open country, sky-blue above and rusty-orange below, that nests in tree holes and nest boxes. Its comeback after mid-20th-century declines is one of the great successes of backyard conservation.
nativeRange: Eastern North America from southern Canada to the Gulf coast, with resident populations in the highlands of Mexico and Central America to Nicaragua
abilities: Spots insects in grass from a perch at up to tens of metres and drops onto them
Raises two or three broods a year, with earlier young sometimes helping feed later ones
Readily adopts nest boxes, which helped it recover after starlings and House Sparrows took natural cavities

animal.diet: Ground insects such as grasshoppers, crickets and beetles; berries in winter
animal.habitat: Meadows, pastures, orchards, golf courses and open pine woods with scattered perches
animal.behaviour: Bluebird 'trails' of nest boxes along roadsides and fences, promoted by the North American Bluebird Society (founded 1978), now support a large share of the population.
fieldMarks: Male: vivid royal-blue upperparts, rusty-orange throat and breast, white belly
Female: greyish above with blue wings and tail, paler orange breast
Upright posture on wires and fence posts
Juveniles grey-brown with spotted breasts and blue in the wings
animal.voice: A soft, low, gurgling warble, often rendered 'tur-a-lee, tur-a-lee'; call a gentle 'tu-a-wee'.
animal.lookalikes: Western Bluebird has a blue (not orange) throat and often a rusty back. Mountain Bluebird lacks orange. Indigo Bunting is blue all over with a conical bill.
animal.whereToSee: Nest-box trails, pastures and golf courses across the eastern US; easy in winter in the south-east.
animal.season: Resident in the southern US; summer visitor in the north, Mar–Oct

lore: Henry David Thoreau wrote in his journal that 'the bluebird carries the sky on his back'; it is the state bird of Missouri and New York.
funFact: Like the blue jay's, its blue is structural: tiny air pockets in the feathers scatter blue light, and a crushed feather looks brown.

summary: A small finch whose summer males glow lemon-yellow with a black cap. It is among the strictest vegetarians of North American songbirds and waits until late summer to nest, when thistles have gone to seed.
nativeRange: Southern Canada and the United States; winters south to northern Mexico
abilities: Feeds its young almost entirely on regurgitated seeds
Lines nests with thistle down so tightly woven they can hold water
Moults its body feathers twice a year, switching between bright breeding and dull winter plumage
Brown-headed Cowbird chicks raised in goldfinch nests rarely survive on the seed diet

animal.diet: Seeds of thistles, sunflowers, asters and other composites; nyjer and sunflower at feeders
animal.habitat: Weedy fields, roadsides, floodplains, orchards and gardens
animal.behaviour: It flies in deep, bouncing undulations, calling on each rise.
fieldMarks: Breeding male: bright yellow with black cap, black wings with white bars, white undertail
Female and winter birds: dull olive-buff with black wings and pale wing bars
Short, conical pink-orange bill in summer
Notched black-and-white tail
animal.voice: A long, canary-like series of twitters and warbles; flight call 'po-ta-to-chip', 'per-chic-o-ree'.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser Goldfinch (west) has a greenish or black back and yellow undertail. Pine Siskin is streaky brown with yellow wing flashes. Yellow Warbler has a thin bill and no black.
animal.whereToSee: Thistle and nyjer feeders across the US; weedy fields with coneflowers and sunflowers in late summer.
animal.season: Resident across much of the US; northern birds move south in winter

lore: It is the state bird of Iowa, New Jersey and Washington, chosen in Washington by a schoolchildren's vote.
funFact: It nests later than almost any other North American songbird, often starting in July.

summary: A neat, grey-hooded sparrow whose arrival at feeders signals winter across much of the US — hence the nickname 'snowbird'. Its many regional forms evolved strikingly different colours in only the last several thousand years.
nativeRange: Breeds across Canada, Alaska and the mountains of the western and north-eastern US; winters throughout most of the US and northern Mexico
abilities: Flashes white outer tail feathers in flight, a signal used in both courtship and alarm
Has diversified into distinct forms — Slate-colored, Oregon, Pink-sided, White-winged, Gray-headed — since the last glaciation
Has colonised urban habitats; a population in San Diego evolved less white in the tail within a few decades

animal.diet: Seeds of grasses and weeds; insects in summer
animal.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forest when breeding; open woods, fields and gardens in winter
animal.behaviour: Wintering flocks keep a pecking order, and birds of different forms often mix at the same feeder.
fieldMarks: Slate-grey or black hood with a pale pink bill
White belly sharply cut off from the dark breast
Bright white outer tail feathers flashed in flight
Western 'Oregon' form has a black hood and brown back
animal.voice: A musical trill on one pitch, like a Chipping Sparrow but more ringing; calls a sharp 'tack' and twittering in flight.
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-eyed Junco (south-eastern Arizona and Mexico) has yellow eyes and a rufous back. Eastern Towhee is larger with rufous sides. Chipping Sparrow's trill is drier and faster.
animal.whereToSee: Winter feeders and woodland edges across the US; breeding in the Appalachians, Rockies, Sierra Nevada and boreal Canada.
animal.season: Winter visitor (Oct–Apr) in most of the US; resident in western and Appalachian mountains

funFact: Its species name hyemalis means 'of winter'.

summary: A streaky brown sparrow that sings from shrubs in almost every brushy habitat in North America. It varies so much across its range that dozens of subspecies are recognised, from small pale desert birds to large dark Aleutian ones.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada south through the US to central Mexico
abilities: Each male sings a repertoire of roughly 5–13 song types, learned from neighbours
Neighbouring males 'match' each other's song types during territorial disputes
Varies dramatically in size and colour across its range in step with climate
Breeds from salt marshes and desert streams to subarctic islands

animal.diet: Insects in summer; seeds and fruit in winter
animal.habitat: Brushy fields, streamsides, marsh edges, hedgerows and gardens
animal.behaviour: In flight it pumps its long, rounded tail up and down.
fieldMarks: Brown upperparts and white underparts with heavy streaks merging into a central breast spot
Broad grey eyebrow and brown stripe behind the eye
Dark malar (moustache) stripe
Long, rounded tail pumped in flight
animal.voice: Opens with two or three clear notes, then a buzzy trill and jumble — remembered as 'Maids, maids, maids, put on your tea-kettle-ettle-ettle'; call a nasal 'chimp'.
animal.lookalikes: Savannah Sparrow has a yellowish eyebrow, finer streaks and a short notched tail. Lincoln's Sparrow is finely streaked on a buffy breast. Fox Sparrow is larger with heavier triangular spots.
animal.whereToSee: Shrubby edges and wetlands across North America; one of the first songs of late winter in the eastern US.
animal.season: Resident in much of the US; northern birds migrate south for winter

lore: Margaret Morse Nice's years of observation of individually banded song sparrows in her Columbus, Ohio, backyard, published as Studies in the Life History of the Song Sparrow (1937), became a landmark of bird behaviour science.
funFact: The Aleutian Island birds can weigh about four times as much as the smallest desert populations.

summary: One of the most abundant birds in North America, whose glossy black males flare scarlet shoulder patches from every cattail marsh in spring. Males defend territories that may hold many nesting females.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada south through the US, Mexico and Central America to Costa Rica; also the Bahamas and Cuba
abilities: Highly polygynous: one male's territory can host up to about 15 nesting females
Males can cover their red epaulets to slip through rivals' territories unchallenged
Gathers in winter roosts that can number in the millions together with grackles, cowbirds and starlings
Mobs hawks, crows and people near its nests

animal.diet: Insects in summer; seeds and grain in winter
animal.habitat: Cattail and bulrush marshes, ditches, wet fields, pastures
animal.behaviour: Males return north weeks before females and sing from cattails even in snow.
fieldMarks: Male: glossy black with red shoulder patch bordered by yellow
Female: heavily streaked dark brown, sparrow-like, often with a peachy face
Sharp, conical, pointed bill
Males puff and spread the epaulets while singing
animal.voice: A gurgling 'conk-la-ree!' or 'oak-a-lee!' ending in a trill; calls a sharp 'check' and a whistled alarm.
animal.lookalikes: Tricolored Blackbird (California) has a darker red patch with a white border. Female could be mistaken for a large sparrow, but the long pointed bill differs. 'Bicolored' males in California lack the yellow border.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any marsh, roadside ditch or wet meadow in North America from March onwards.
animal.season: Resident in the south; summer visitor in the north, Mar–Oct

lore: Mark Catesby painted it in the 1730s as 'The Red-wing'd Starling'.
funFact: Its genus name Agelaius means 'belonging to a flock'.

summary: A rare, tail-pumping warbler that nests only in young jack pine stands on sandy soils, mostly in northern Michigan, and winters in the Bahamas. It fell to fewer than 200 singing males in the 1970s and recovered through habitat management and cowbird control.
nativeRange: Breeds mainly in northern Lower Michigan, with small numbers in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, Wisconsin and Ontario; winters in the Bahamas and Turks and Caicos
abilities: Depends on jack pine stands roughly 5–20 years old, a habitat historically created by wildfire
Nests on the ground beneath the low living branches of young pines
Constantly bobs its tail while foraging
Migrates about 2,000 km between Michigan and the Bahamas

animal.diet: Insects and larvae; fruit on the wintering grounds
animal.habitat: Dense young jack pine on sandy outwash plains; low scrub in the Bahamas
animal.behaviour: Brown-headed Cowbird parasitism once affected most nests; trapping cowbirds from 1972 was key to recovery.
fieldMarks: Blue-grey upperparts streaked with black
Bright yellow throat and breast, black streaks on the sides
Broken white eye-ring; males have black lores
Constant tail-pumping
animal.voice: A loud, low-pitched, rich chatter rising at the end, e.g. 'chip-chip-che-way-o'.
animal.lookalikes: Magnolia Warbler has a white wing patch and a white tail band. Prairie Warbler also pumps its tail but is smaller with a yellow face and olive back. Canada Warbler has a necklace and no streaks above.
animal.whereToSee: Guided tours from Grayling (Michigan Audubon) and Mio (US Forest Service), Michigan, May–early July; Bahamian islands such as Eleuthera in winter.
animal.season: Breeds in Michigan May–Aug; winters in the Bahamas Oct–Apr

lore: It is named for Jared Potter Kirtland, the Ohio naturalist on whose farm near Cleveland the first specimen was collected in 1851; it was removed from the US endangered species list in 2019 after decades of recovery work.
funFact: Its nesting grounds were not discovered until 1903, when a nest was found in Oscoda County, Michigan.

summary: A shy brown thrush with a rusty tail whose ethereal, echoing song is often called the most beautiful in North America. It is the only spotted thrush that commonly winters in the United States.
nativeRange: Breeds across Alaska, Canada, the north-eastern US and western mountains; winters in the southern US, Mexico and Central America to Guatemala
abilities: Each song begins with a long, clear note at a new pitch, followed by a cascade of flute-like phrases
Song intervals follow simple harmonic ratios similar to those of human musical scales, according to a 2014 study in PNAS
Switches from insects to fruit such as holly and dogwood in winter

animal.diet: Ground insects, spiders and worms; berries in winter
animal.habitat: Conifer and mixed forests when breeding; woodland understorey in winter
animal.behaviour: It habitually raises its tail and lowers it slowly while flicking its wings.
fieldMarks: Warm reddish tail contrasting with olive-brown or greyish back
Spotted breast, spots smaller and smudgier than a Wood Thrush's
Thin, complete whitish eye-ring
Slow tail-raising habit
animal.voice: A clear, sustained opening whistle followed by a spiralling cascade of flute-like notes, each song at a different pitch; call a low 'chuck'.
animal.lookalikes: Swainson's Thrush has buffy 'spectacles' and a uniform brown tail. Veery is tawny with faint spots. Wood Thrush is rufous on the head, with bold round spots. Fox Sparrow has a conical bill.
animal.whereToSee: Northern and mountain conifer forests in summer (e.g. Adirondacks, Green Mountains, Rockies); southern US woodlands in winter.
animal.season: Summer visitor in the north, Apr–Oct; winter visitor in the south, Oct–Apr

lore: In Walt Whitman's elegy for Abraham Lincoln, 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd' (1865), a hermit thrush sings from the swamp; it is Vermont's state bird.
funFact: Its genus name Catharus comes from Greek katharos, 'pure' or 'clean'.

summary: A plain, rufous ovenbird that builds a domed nest of mud and straw shaped like a traditional clay bread oven. Pairs stay together for years and duet loudly, and it is the national bird of Argentina.
nativeRange: Eastern and central South America: Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay and northern and central Argentina
abilities: Builds a heavy, oven-shaped nest of mud, dung and plant fibre with a curved inner wall separating the entrance from the egg chamber
Constructs a nest in a few weeks using thousands of beakfuls of wet mud, often after rain
Old nests are reused by other birds such as Saffron Finches, swallows and parakeets
Mated pairs sing synchronised, shrill duets

animal.diet: Insects, worms and other invertebrates gleaned from the ground
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees, pastures, roadsides and city parks
animal.behaviour: Nests are placed on posts, branches, utility poles and even street lamps, in full view.
fieldMarks: Rufous-brown upperparts with a brighter rufous tail
Pale buffy underparts with a whitish throat
Slender, slightly decurved bill
Walks deliberately on the ground with a high-stepping gait
animal.voice: Loud, shrill, accelerating series of notes, often given as a duet by the pair, which sing with wings drooped and quivering.
animal.lookalikes: Pale-legged Hornero (north and west) has pale legs and a whitish eyebrow. Crested Hornero has a small crest and is found in Paraguay and Argentina's Chaco. Thrushes have a different bill shape and do not walk.
animal.whereToSee: Parks and farmland around Buenos Aires, Montevideo and southern Brazil; abundant in the Pampas and Pantanal.

lore: Argentina's national bird since 1928, it appears widely in gaucho folklore as a model of the hard-working household.
funFact: Its mud nests can last several years and weigh several kilograms.

summary: A blazing orange-red cotinga of Andean cloud forest ravines whose males gather at dawn leks, bowing, bobbing and squealing to attract drab females. It is Peru's national bird.
nativeRange: Eastern and western slopes of the Andes from Venezuela and Colombia through Ecuador and Peru to Bolivia, mainly 500–2,400 m
abilities: Males display at communal leks, each defending a small court and performing in front of visiting females
Females build mud-and-plant cup nests glued to rock faces in humid gorges
Important seed disperser for fruiting cloud-forest trees
Takes small vertebrates such as frogs and lizards as well as fruit

animal.diet: Mainly fruit; insects, frogs and small lizards
animal.habitat: Humid montane forest near rocky streams and ravines
animal.behaviour: Females raise the young alone; males spend much of the breeding season at the lek.
fieldMarks: Male: brilliant scarlet or orange body with a disc-shaped crest that hides the bill
Black wings and tail, with pale silvery-grey tertials
Female: dark brownish-orange with a smaller crest
Plump, pigeon-sized shape
animal.voice: At leks, loud nasal squawks, grunts and pig-like squeals; otherwise mostly silent.
animal.lookalikes: Guianan Cock-of-the-rock (Guiana Shield east of the Andes) is orange with a fringed crest and white wing patches; their ranges do not overlap. No other Andean bird has the crest-covered bill.
animal.whereToSee: Lek sites along Peru's Manu Road (Cock-of-the-rock Lodge), near Mindo in Ecuador, and in Colombia's Río Claro and cloud forests.
animal.season: Resident year-round; leks most active at dawn and late afternoon

lore: Known in Quechua as tunki, it was named Peru's national bird and features in Andean folk dances and textiles.
funFact: The genus name Rupicola means 'rock-dweller', from the female's habit of nesting on cliff faces.

summary: A pure white cotinga with a long, fleshy black wattle dangling from its bill, it has the loudest bird call ever measured — about 125 decibels. Males aim the blast directly at females perched close by.
nativeRange: Guiana Shield of Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and northern Brazil, with an isolated population south of the Amazon in Pará
abilities: Produces calls measured at about 125 dB at close range, louder than the Screaming Piha (Podos & Cohn-Haft, Current Biology, 2019)
Swings its head and wattle as it delivers the second note of its call toward a female
Swallows fruits whole and regurgitates seeds, dispersing forest trees

animal.diet: Fruit, especially of trees in the laurel family
animal.habitat: Canopy of humid hill and montane forest
animal.behaviour: Males call from exposed perches high in the canopy for hours each day.
fieldMarks: Male: entirely white, with a single long black fleshy wattle hanging from the forehead over the bill
Female: olive-green above with yellowish, olive-streaked underparts
Large dark eye and broad bill
Stocky, pigeon-like shape
animal.voice: Ear-splitting, bell-like notes — a two-part 'kong-kay' or a single metallic 'boing' that can be heard over long distances.
animal.lookalikes: Bearded Bellbird has a brown head and many short wattles on the throat. Bare-throated Bellbird (Atlantic Forest) has a bare blue-green throat. Three-wattled Bellbird (Central America) is chestnut with a white head and neck and three wattles.
animal.whereToSee: Hill forests of the Guiana Shield, e.g. the tepui foothills of Venezuela, the Iwokrama and Kaieteur areas of Guyana, and Roraima in Brazil.
animal.season: Resident; calling peaks in the breeding season

funFact: Researchers found the loudest calls are the shortest, suggesting a trade-off between volume and duration.

summary: A small Amazonian canopy tanager painted in lime-green, black, scarlet, turquoise and violet. Despite its scientific name, it has never lived in Chile.
nativeRange: Amazon Basin and eastern Andean foothills, from Colombia and Venezuela through Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, the Guianas and Amazonian Brazil
abilities: Travels in noisy groups at the core of mixed-species canopy flocks
Searches undersides of leaves and twigs for insects while hanging acrobatically
Disperses small seeds of fruiting trees and epiphytes

animal.diet: Small fruits and berries; insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Canopy and edges of humid lowland and foothill forest, up to about 1,600 m
animal.behaviour: Groups of 5–10 often lead the mixed flocks that sweep through the Amazon canopy each morning.
fieldMarks: Shining apple-green head contrasting with velvety black back
Scarlet (or, in some populations, red-and-yellow) rump
Turquoise-blue underparts and violet-blue throat
Black wings and tail
animal.voice: High, thin 'tsit' and 'zeet' notes given constantly by flocks; no well-developed song.
animal.lookalikes: Seven-colored Tanager (Atlantic Forest of Brazil) has a turquoise-green head, black throat and orange rump; ranges do not overlap. Green-and-gold Tanager is largely green-gold without the black back.
animal.whereToSee: Canopy towers and forest edges in Amazonian Ecuador (Sacha, Yasuní), Peru (Tambopata, Manu) and Brazil (Cristalino).

lore: Nicholas Vigors named it chilensis in 1832, apparently because the specimens reached Europe from a dealer who mislabelled them as Chilean.
funFact: Its Brazilian name sete-cores means 'seven colours'.

summary: A tiny Andean manakin whose males 'sing' with their wings. Specialised, club-shaped feathers rub together like a bow on a violin string, producing a sustained high note.
nativeRange: Western slope of the Andes in Colombia and Ecuador (the Chocó region)
abilities: Males produce a tonal note near 1,500 Hz by rubbing modified secondary feathers together over 100 times a second (Bostwick & Prum, Science, 2005)
One wing feather bears a row of ridges and another a stiff tip, like a comb and pick
Unlike almost all other birds, it has solid rather than hollow wing bones, which help support the vibrating feathers

animal.diet: Small fruits and insects
animal.habitat: Understorey and mid-levels of humid foothill and subtropical forest
animal.behaviour: Males display on perches within earshot of each other, flicking their wings above the back to make the sound.
fieldMarks: Male: rich chestnut body with a bright red crown
Black and white in the wings; white on the inner wing visible in display
Female: olive-green with a cinnamon-tinged face
Tiny, short-tailed manakin shape
animal.voice: A mechanical 'tik-tik-ting': two sharp clicks followed by a ringing, violin-like whine made by the wings.
animal.lookalikes: Striped Manakin has a red crown but a red-streaked belly and no chestnut body. Other manakins in its range lack the chestnut-and-red male plumage.
animal.whereToSee: Mindo and Milpe Bird Sanctuary in north-western Ecuador; Chocó foothill reserves in Colombia.

funFact: Its wing sound was first analysed with high-speed video, which showed the feathers vibrating faster than the bird can beat its wings.

summary: The only bird whose bill is longer than its body, excluding the tail. It reaches nectar at the bottom of long-tubed Andean flowers that no other hummingbird can use.
nativeRange: Andes from western Venezuela and Colombia through Ecuador and Peru to Bolivia, mostly 1,700–3,500 m
abilities: Bill about 9–11 cm long, longer than the bird's head and body
Main pollinator of long-tubed flowers such as Passiflora mixta and angel's trumpets (Brugmansia)
Perches with its bill pointed steeply upward to balance the weight
Grooms with its feet because it cannot reach its feathers with its bill

animal.diet: Nectar from long tubular flowers; small insects caught in flight
animal.habitat: Humid montane forest edge and shrubby clearings
animal.behaviour: It catches insects on the wing with its mouth open wide, keeping the long bill out of the way.
fieldMarks: Extremely long, straight, slightly upturned bill
Bronze-green body; male with coppery head
Forked, greenish-bronze tail
Small white spot behind the eye
animal.voice: A low, rattling 'trrr' and buzzy chips; no complex song.
animal.lookalikes: No other hummingbird has a bill nearly as long. Great Sapphirewing and incas share its habitat but have short or medium bills.
animal.whereToSee: Feeders and flowering edges at Yanacocha Reserve and Guango Lodge (Ecuador), Abra Málaga and Wayqecha (Peru).

funFact: It co-evolved with Passiflora mixta, whose floral tube is long enough that only the sword-bill can reach its nectar.

summary: A nocturnal insect-eater that spends the day perched bolt upright on a broken branch, so perfectly camouflaged it looks like part of the tree. At night its mournful, falling song is one of the most haunting sounds of the Neotropics.
nativeRange: Southern Central America (Nicaragua and Costa Rica) through South America to northern Argentina and Uruguay; Trinidad and Tobago
abilities: Freezes motionless on a stump with bill pointed skyward, mimicking a dead branch
Notches in its eyelids let it watch for predators with eyes apparently closed
Huge gape catches large flying insects in sallies from a perch
Lays a single egg in a shallow depression on top of a broken branch, with no nest

animal.diet: Large flying insects — moths, beetles, katydids
animal.habitat: Open forest, edges, savanna, plantations and mangroves
animal.behaviour: It returns to the same daytime perch for weeks, which makes it findable once located.
fieldMarks: Mottled grey-brown bark-like plumage
Large yellow eyes; tiny bill above an enormous mouth
Long tail; upright posture on stumps
Dark spots on the breast
animal.voice: A series of 5–8 loud, melancholy whistles falling in pitch and volume, like 'poor-me-one, poor-me-one'.
animal.lookalikes: Northern Potoo (Mexico to Costa Rica, and Jamaica and Hispaniola) is nearly identical but gives a harsh, croaking call. Great Potoo is larger and paler with a growling roar. Nightjars perch lengthwise on branches or rest on the ground.
animal.whereToSee: Pantanal (Brazil), Llanos (Venezuela), Asa Wright Nature Centre (Trinidad) and Amazonian lodges where guides know day roosts.
animal.season: Resident; sings most on moonlit nights

lore: A widespread Guaraní legend tells of a young woman whose lover was killed and who was turned into the urutau, forever crying her grief through the night.
funFact: Its Brazilian name 'mother of the moon' comes from its habit of calling on moonlit nights.

summary: The world's only nocturnal flying fruit-eating bird, it roosts and nests in pitch-dark caves and navigates by echolocation using audible clicks. Its fat-laden chicks were once boiled down for lamp and cooking oil.
nativeRange: Northern and western South America — Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Guyana — and Trinidad
abilities: Echolocates in total darkness with clicks around 2 kHz, audible to humans
Finds fruit at night partly by smell and with large, light-sensitive eyes
Disperses seeds of palms and laurels over long distances
Chicks grow much heavier than adults on a fatty fruit diet before slimming down to fledge

animal.diet: Oily fruits of palms, laurels and incense trees, plucked in flight
animal.habitat: Caves and gorges near forest, from sea level to about 3,400 m
animal.behaviour: Colonies of thousands leave caves at dusk and may forage over 100 km away in a night.
fieldMarks: Rich rufous-brown plumage with white spots on wings and head
Strongly hooked bill fringed with long rictal bristles
Long, broad wings and long tail
Large dark eyes
animal.voice: Deafening screams, snarls and clicks inside roost caves; the screams inspired the Spanish name guácharo, 'one who wails'.
animal.lookalikes: Potoos and nightjars are greyer, have tiny bills, and do not roost in caves; no other cave-dwelling bird in its range is as large.
animal.whereToSee: Cueva del Guácharo National Park (Caripe, Venezuela), Dunston Cave at Asa Wright Nature Centre (Trinidad), and the Cueva de los Tayos region (Ecuador).

lore: Alexander von Humboldt visited the Cueva del Guácharo near Caripe in 1799 and described how the local Chaima people harvested chicks for their fat; the species' name caripensis honours the site.
funFact: Fat oilbird chicks can weigh about 50% more than their parents.

summary: A crow-sized black woodpecker with a flaming red crest that chisels large rectangular holes into trees in search of carpenter ants. Its old cavities become homes for owls, ducks, bats and martens.
nativeRange: Much of Canada, the eastern United States and the Pacific Northwest
abilities: Excavates rectangular holes up to tens of centimetres long to reach carpenter ant galleries
Its abandoned nest holes are used by Wood Ducks, owls, flying squirrels and bats
Uses a long, barbed tongue to extract ants
Drums slowly and loudly on resonant trunks to claim territory

animal.diet: Carpenter ants, beetle larvae, other insects; fruit and nuts
animal.habitat: Mature forest with large trees and dead wood; increasingly suburban woodlots
animal.behaviour: Pairs hold territories year-round and excavate a new nest cavity each spring.
fieldMarks: Mostly black body with a bright red, pointed crest
Bold white stripes on the face and neck
Large white underwing linings flashing in flight
Male has a red moustache stripe; female's is black
animal.voice: A loud, wild, ringing 'wuk-wuk-wuk-wuk', rising and falling; drumming deep and slow, trailing off.
animal.lookalikes: Ivory-billed Woodpecker, if it survives, has an ivory bill and white trailing edges to the upper wing. Red-headed Woodpecker is much smaller with an all-red head and white wing patches.
animal.whereToSee: Large tracts of mature forest across the eastern US and Pacific Northwest; listen for its call in places like the Great Smoky Mountains or Congaree National Park.

lore: Mark Catesby painted it in the 1730s as 'The larger red-crested Wood-pecker'; its rectangular excavations were used by early naturalists as a sign of its presence.
funFact: Woody Woodpecker's look is often linked to this species, though the cartoon's creator, Walter Lantz, was said to be inspired by an Acorn Woodpecker.

summary: A large brown woodpecker that feeds mostly on the ground, licking up ants. In flight it flashes golden-yellow or salmon-red under its wings and a bold white rump.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada through the US and Mexico to Nicaragua; also Cuba and Grand Cayman
abilities: Ants and their larvae make up nearly half its diet, more than any other North American woodpecker
Has a long tongue coated in sticky saliva for collecting ants from the soil
Two forms — eastern Yellow-shafted and western Red-shafted — hybridise across a broad zone on the Great Plains

animal.diet: Ants and beetles; fruit and seeds in winter
animal.habitat: Open woods, parks, edges and burned forest
animal.behaviour: It often drums on metal chimney caps and gutters, which amplify the sound.
fieldMarks: Brown, black-barred back; buff breast with black spots
Black crescent bib
White rump in flight
Yellow (east) or salmon-red (west) wing and tail shafts; males have a black or red moustache
animal.voice: A long, loud 'wik-wik-wik-wik'; also a piercing 'kleer' and a soft 'wicka-wicka' in courtship.
animal.lookalikes: Gilded Flicker (Sonoran Desert) has yellow underwings with a cinnamon crown. Red-bellied Woodpecker has a barred back without a bib. In flight the white rump can recall Red-headed Woodpecker, which has white wing patches instead.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, parks and open woods across North America; often seen feeding on the ground.
animal.season: Resident in much of the US; northern birds migrate south in autumn

lore: It is Alabama's state bird; Confederate soldiers from Alabama were nicknamed 'yellowhammers' after the yellow trim on their uniforms.
funFact: It is one of the few North American woodpeckers that regularly migrates.

summary: A toucan with a huge rainbow-coloured bill — green, blue, orange and red — and a sulphur-yellow bib. It is the national bird of Belize.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to northern Colombia and north-western Venezuela
abilities: Its bill is light — keratin over a honeycomb of bone and fibres — despite being about a third of the bird's length
Tosses fruit into the air and catches it in its throat
Disperses large seeds of rainforest trees
Groups sleep in tree holes with tails folded over their backs

animal.diet: Mainly fruit; also insects, lizards, eggs and nestlings
animal.habitat: Canopy of lowland tropical forest and edges, up to about 1,900 m
animal.behaviour: Small flocks travel through the canopy in follow-the-leader flights of a few flaps and a glide.
fieldMarks: Large, multicoloured bill: lime-green, with blue, orange and a red tip
Bright yellow face, throat and chest
Black body with red undertail coverts and white rump
Lime-green bare skin around the eye
animal.voice: A dry, frog-like croaking 'krrrek-krrrek', repeated monotonously.
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-throated Toucan has a two-tone dark-and-yellow bill and a yelping call. Collared Aracari is smaller with a red-banded yellow belly.
animal.whereToSee: Tikal (Guatemala), Cockscomb Basin and Crooked Tree (Belize), Costa Rica's Caribbean lowlands such as Tortuguero.

funFact: It is the cartoon model for Toucan Sam, the Froot Loops mascot.

summary: The largest toucan, with an enormous orange bill tipped in black. Unlike most toucans it lives in open savanna and woodland, and uses its bill as a radiator to shed body heat.
nativeRange: Guianas, Brazil (excluding most of the Amazon rainforest interior), eastern Bolivia, Paraguay and northern Argentina
abilities: Regulates blood flow to its bill to dump heat; the bill can account for a large share of total heat loss (Tattersall et al., Science, 2009)
Bill about 19–23 cm long yet very light
Raids nests of other birds for eggs and nestlings
Disperses seeds of Cerrado and Pantanal trees

animal.diet: Fruit, insects, eggs, nestlings and small reptiles
animal.habitat: Savanna, open woodland, palm groves, plantations and towns
animal.behaviour: It tucks its bill under its back feathers while sleeping, which reduces heat loss on cool nights.
fieldMarks: Huge, bright orange bill with a black tip and a black spot at the base
Black body with white throat and bib
Orange bare skin around the eye, with a blue eye-ring
White uppertail and red undertail coverts
animal.voice: A deep, grunting, croaking 'grrr-grrr' or 'groonk', often in series.
animal.lookalikes: White-throated (Red-billed) Toucan has a dark reddish bill with a yellow ridge and lives in rainforest. Channel-billed Toucan has a black bill with a blue base.
animal.whereToSee: The Pantanal (Mato Grosso), Iguaçu Falls, Emas National Park and towns of the Brazilian Cerrado.

lore: The word 'toucan' comes through Portuguese from the Tupi name for the bird; early European naturalists in Brazil, including Georg Marcgrave in the 1640s, described and drew toucans.
funFact: In the Pantanal it is both the main seed disperser of the manduvi tree — the Hyacinth Macaw's main nest tree — and a major predator of Hyacinth Macaw eggs.

summary: A ground-dwelling cuckoo of the deserts and scrub of the south-western US and Mexico that runs down lizards, snakes and scorpions. It can sprint at about 30 km/h and kills rattlesnakes by beating them against rocks.
nativeRange: South-western and south-central US (expanding into Missouri, Arkansas and Louisiana) and northern and central Mexico
abilities: Runs at around 30 km/h, steering with its long tail
Eats venomous prey including rattlesnakes and scorpions
Sunbathes with back feathers raised to expose black skin, warming up after cold nights
Excretes excess salt through a gland near the eye, conserving water

animal.diet: Lizards, snakes, insects, scorpions, rodents, small birds; some fruit
animal.habitat: Arid scrub, desert, chaparral, open grassland with cover
animal.behaviour: Courting males present food, such as a lizard, to the female before mating.
fieldMarks: Long, white-tipped tail often cocked up
Shaggy dark crest and streaky brown-and-white plumage
Long, heavy bill; bare blue and orange skin behind the eye
Long legs with X-shaped zygodactyl footprints (two toes forward, two back)
animal.voice: A series of slow, descending, dove-like coos 'coo-coo-coo-oo'; also loud bill-clattering.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser Roadrunner (Mexico and Central America) is smaller with a less streaked throat. Ring-necked Pheasant has a short bill and lacks streaks.
animal.whereToSee: Desert parks of Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas — e.g. Big Bend National Park, Sonoran Desert around Tucson, Bosque del Apache.

lore: Pueblo peoples used its X-shaped footprints as a protective symbol, since the tracks do not show which way the bird went; it is New Mexico's state bird.
funFact: Real roadrunners top out around 30 km/h — fast for a bird on foot, but slower than a coyote.

summary: North America's most familiar large hawk, often seen perched on roadside poles or soaring over fields. Its hoarse scream is the sound film-makers dub in for almost any bird of prey, including Bald Eagles.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada through the US, Mexico and Central America to Panama; the West Indies
abilities: Hunts by watching from a high perch or 'kiting' motionless into the wind
Plumage varies from very pale to almost black across many regional forms and morphs
Has adapted to cities, nesting on building ledges
Pairs often stay together for years and reuse nests

animal.diet: Rodents, rabbits, squirrels; also birds, snakes and carrion
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered perches, from deserts to farmland and city parks
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform high soaring courtship flights, with the male diving and climbing and sometimes dangling his legs.
fieldMarks: Adult tail brick-red above, pale pinkish below
Dark band of streaks across the pale belly
Dark bar (patagial mark) on the leading edge of the underwing
Broad, rounded wings and short wide tail; dark and rufous morphs occur, especially in the West
animal.voice: A hoarse, rasping, descending scream 'kee-eeee-arrr', 2–3 seconds long.
animal.lookalikes: Red-shouldered Hawk has a banded black-and-white tail and pale wing 'windows'. Rough-legged Hawk has black wrist patches and a white tail base. Swainson's Hawk has dark flight feathers below and a brown bib. Juvenile Red-tails have brown banded tails.
animal.whereToSee: Highway edges and fields almost anywhere in North America; hawk-watch sites such as Hawk Mountain (Pennsylvania) and Duluth's Hawk Ridge in autumn.
animal.season: Resident in most of the US; northern birds migrate Sep–Nov

lore: A red-tailed hawk nicknamed Pale Male nested on a Fifth Avenue apartment building in New York City from the early 1990s, becoming one of the most famous wild birds in the world.
funFact: It was first scientifically described from a specimen collected in Jamaica, hence jamaicensis.

summary: The most powerful raptor of the Americas, a rainforest eagle that snatches sloths and monkeys from the canopy. Its hind talons are as long as a grizzly bear's claws, and a pair raises a single chick only every two to three years.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico (now very rare) through Central America to eastern Bolivia, Brazil and north-eastern Argentina
abilities: Hind talons can reach about 12–13 cm
Carries prey such as sloths weighing several kilograms
Manoeuvres through dense canopy on short, broad wings rather than soaring high
Nests in giant emergent trees such as kapok (Ceiba) and Brazil nut

animal.diet: Mainly sloths and monkeys; also opossums, porcupines, macaws and iguanas
animal.habitat: Large tracts of undisturbed lowland tropical forest
animal.size: 89–105 cm; wingspan 176–224 cm; females 6–9 kg, males 4–5 kg
animal.behaviour: The single chick depends on its parents for over a year after fledging.
fieldMarks: Pale grey head with a split, double crest
Broad black band across the chest
White underparts with barred thighs and enormous yellow feet
Short, broad wings and long, banded tail
animal.voice: A long, wailing scream 'wheeeee-oo', especially from young birds begging at the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Crested Eagle is smaller and slimmer with a single crest and lighter feet. Juvenile Harpies are whitish and can be confused with juvenile Crested Eagles; check size and leg thickness.
animal.whereToSee: Darién (Panama), Tambopata (Peru), Alta Floresta (Brazil) and Iwokrama (Guyana), usually at known nest trees with local guides.

lore: Named after the harpies, the bird-bodied spirits of Greek myth, it is Panama's national bird and appears on Panama's coat of arms.
funFact: Its facial disc of feathers may help funnel sound to its ears, like an owl's.

summary: A long-legged, eagle-like falcon with a bare red face that walks the ground scavenging and hunting. It is as likely to be found at a roadkill or behind a plough as on the wing.
nativeRange: Florida, Texas and Arizona south through Mexico, Central America and South America to Tierra del Fuego
abilities: Hunts on foot, turning over debris and dung for insects and small animals
Robs vultures and other birds of food
Follows tractors, fires and cattle to catch flushed prey
Throws its head back over its back while calling

animal.diet: Carrion, insects, small mammals, reptiles, fish and eggs
animal.habitat: Open country — prairies, pastures, savanna, desert scrub
animal.behaviour: Unlike most falcons, it builds its own stick nest, often in palms or cacti.
fieldMarks: Black cap and shaggy crest above bare red-orange to yellow facial skin
Heavy, pale bluish hooked bill
White throat and neck; barred breast; black belly
In flight: white patches near the wingtips and white tail with a black terminal band; long yellow legs
animal.voice: A dry, harsh rattle, given with the head thrown back; the name 'caracara' imitates it.
animal.lookalikes: Black Vulture has a bare grey head and lacks the white neck. Bald Eagle immature lacks the black cap and orange face.
animal.whereToSee: Ranchland of central Florida (Kissimmee Prairie), south Texas, the Pantanal and the Argentine Pampas.

lore: Some historians argue that the bird in the Aztec founding legend of Tenochtitlan — an eagle on a cactus devouring a snake — was a caracara, though Mexico's coat of arms shows a Golden Eagle; in Brazil, João do Vale's 1964 song 'Carcará' made it a symbol of the drought-hardened north-east.
funFact: The Florida population is federally listed as threatened in the US because of the loss of native prairie.

summary: One of the heaviest flying birds on Earth, with a wingspan of over 3 m, it soars over the Andes and Patagonian coast in search of carcasses. It is a national symbol of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia and Ecuador.
nativeRange: Andes from Venezuela and Colombia to Tierra del Fuego, and adjacent Pacific coasts and Patagonian lowlands
abilities: Wingspan up to about 3.3 m and weight up to about 15 kg
A tracking study found condors flapped only about 1% of their flight time, one bird flying over 170 km in five hours without flapping (Williams et al., PNAS, 2020)
Rides thermals and slope winds to cover over 200 km a day
Lays a single egg, usually every two years

animal.diet: Carrion of large mammals — llamas, guanacos, cattle; marine mammal carcasses on the coast
animal.habitat: Open mountains, high plateaus and coasts with cliffs for roosting and nesting
animal.lifespan: Over 50 years; captive birds have exceeded 70
animal.behaviour: Males are larger than females, unusual among raptors, and carry a fleshy comb on the head.
fieldMarks: Black plumage with a white neck ruff
Large white panels on the upper wing (secondaries)
Bare grey-red head; male with a dark fleshy comb (caruncle)
Long, broad wings with deeply 'fingered' primaries
animal.voice: Almost silent; lacking a syrinx-driven song, it hisses and clucks at carcasses and roosts.
animal.lookalikes: California Condor (no range overlap) has white underwing linings rather than upper-wing panels and lacks the white ruff. Black Vulture and Turkey Vulture are far smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Cruz del Cóndor, Colca Canyon (Peru); Torres del Paine (Chile); Quebrada del Condorito (Argentina); the Antisana reserve (Ecuador).
animal.season: Resident year-round; Colca viewing best in the morning, Jun–Oct

lore: For the Inca, the kuntur was a messenger of the upper world (Hanan Pacha), and in the Peruvian Yawar Fiesta a condor was tied to a bull's back to symbolise the struggle of Andean and Spanish cultures.
funFact: Its species name gryphus refers to the griffin of legend.

summary: North America's largest flying land bird, with a wingspan near 3 m. It went extinct in the wild in 1987 when the last wild bird was captured, leaving 27 condors, all in captivity; captive breeding and releases have since rebuilt the population to several hundred.
nativeRange: Formerly much of western North America (Pleistocene range continent-wide); reintroduced in California, Arizona–Utah, northern Baja California and, since 2022, the Pacific Northwest
abilities: Soars for hours on thermals and covers well over 200 km in a day
Wingspan up to about 2.9 m
Can live 60 years or more
Lays one egg every one to two years

animal.diet: Carrion of large mammals — deer, cattle, marine mammals
animal.habitat: Rugged mountains, canyons and coastal ranges with open foraging country
animal.size: 117–134 cm; wingspan up to about 2.9 m; 8–14 kg
animal.behaviour: Wild-released birds carry numbered wing tags and GPS transmitters so biologists can trap and test them for lead poisoning.
fieldMarks: Very large, black, with white triangular linings on the underwing
Adults have a bare orange-pink head; juveniles a dusky grey head
Black ruff of feathers around the neck
Flat, steady soaring with long, fingered primaries; usually carries numbered wing tags
animal.voice: No song; hisses and grunts at carcasses.
animal.lookalikes: Turkey Vulture is much smaller, rocks in flight and shows silvery flight feathers (not white linings). Golden Eagle has a feathered head and a longer tail with no white underwing triangle in adults.
animal.whereToSee: Vermilion Cliffs National Monument and the South Rim of the Grand Canyon (Arizona), Pinnacles National Park and Big Sur (California), Zion National Park (Utah).

lore: The Yurok people of northern California, who call it prey-go-neesh, regard it as a sacred bird; in 2022 the Yurok Tribe began releasing condors in Redwood National Park.
funFact: By the end of 2025 the US Fish and Wildlife Service counted 607 California condors, 392 of them flying free; lead poisoning from ammunition fragments remains the main cause of death.

summary: A creamy-white vulture with a bare head painted orange, purple, red and yellow. Other vultures usually find carcasses first, but the king vulture's powerful bill opens tough hides that smaller species cannot.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina
abilities: Tears open large carcasses, giving other scavengers access
Follows smell-guided Turkey and Yellow-headed Vultures to food hidden under forest canopy
Soars for long periods on flat wings over rainforest

animal.diet: Carrion; occasionally weak or newborn animals
animal.habitat: Lowland forest and adjacent savanna, mainly below 1,500 m
animal.behaviour: At carcasses it usually displaces Black and Turkey Vultures.
fieldMarks: Creamy-white body with black flight feathers and tail
Bare, multicoloured head and neck with an orange fleshy caruncle on the bill
Thick grey ruff
White eye with red eye-ring; juveniles all dark
animal.voice: Generally silent; low croaks and bill-snaps.
animal.lookalikes: Wood Stork has long legs and a long neck in flight. Immature king vultures are dark and resemble Black Vultures but are larger with some colour on the head.
animal.whereToSee: Over rainforest in Belize, Costa Rica (Osa Peninsula), Panama and the Amazon; at feeding stations in Brazil and Costa Rica.

lore: The Maya depicted the king vulture in their codices, and its Nahuatl name cozcacuauhtli also named the 16th day of the Aztec calendar.
funFact: Spanish 'zopilote rey' reflects an old belief that it was the king the other vultures stood back for.

summary: The tufted, yellow-eyed owl of children's books, found from Arctic tree line to tropical forests. It takes prey up to the size of skunks and geese and nests in the dead of winter.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada through the US, Mexico and Central America to South America; in the far south replaced by the Magellanic Horned Owl
abilities: Hunts one of the widest prey ranges of any bird — from insects to skunks, ospreys and other owls
Regularly kills skunks, possibly helped by a weak sense of smell
Silent flight from serrated, velvety flight feathers
Begins nesting in January or February, often in old hawk or crow nests

animal.diet: Rabbits, rodents, skunks, birds including waterfowl and other raptors, reptiles
animal.habitat: Almost any habitat with trees, cliffs or structures to roost and nest
animal.behaviour: Mated pairs duet at dusk in winter, the female's hoots higher than the male's despite her larger size.
fieldMarks: Large, bulky owl with widely spaced ear tufts
Yellow eyes in a rusty-orange facial disc rimmed with black
White throat bib
Fine horizontal barring on the underparts
animal.voice: Deep, soft, stuttering hoots, e.g. 'hoo-h'HOO-hoo-hoo'; juveniles give a rasping hiss-scream.
animal.lookalikes: Long-eared Owl is slim with close-set tufts and vertical streaks below. Barred Owl has no tufts and dark eyes. Eastern and Western Screech-Owls have tufts but are tiny.
animal.whereToSee: Parks, woodlots and deserts throughout the Americas; often seen on winter evenings on nest platforms in cottonwoods or on saguaros.

lore: In much of Mesoamerica the owl (Nahuatl tecolotl) was associated with Mictlantecuhtli, lord of the underworld, and its call with death — a belief still voiced in the Mexican saying 'cuando el tecolote canta, el indio muere'.
funFact: Like other owls it cannot move its eyes in their sockets, so it turns its whole head — up to about 270 degrees.

summary: A small, long-legged owl that lives underground in burrows dug by prairie dogs, ground squirrels or armadillos, and is often active by day. It bobs and stares from the burrow mouth, and decorates its entrance with dung to attract beetles.
nativeRange: Western North America and Florida south through Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America to Tierra del Fuego
abilities: Spreads mammal dung around its burrow, which attracts dung beetles it then eats (Levey et al., Nature, 2004)
Chicks in the burrow give a hiss that resembles a rattlesnake's rattle
Florida birds dig their own burrows; western birds usually take over mammal burrows
Hunts both day and night, hovering and running after insects

animal.diet: Insects (beetles, grasshoppers), small rodents, lizards, frogs
animal.habitat: Open, short-grass country — prairies, deserts, pastures, airports, vacant lots
animal.lifespan: Up to about 9 years in the wild
animal.behaviour: It bobs its head and body rapidly when alarmed, a characteristic gesture.
fieldMarks: Small brown owl with white spots, standing on long, sparsely feathered legs
Round head with no ear tufts
Bright yellow eyes beneath bold white eyebrows
White chin stripe; usually seen on the ground or a low post
animal.voice: A soft, two-note 'coo-coooo' at night; chattering and clucking alarm calls.
animal.lookalikes: Short-eared Owl is larger, longer-winged and flies low over grass. Screech-owls have ear tufts and live in trees.
animal.whereToSee: Cape Coral, Florida; prairie dog towns of the Great Plains; Salton Sea agricultural fields (California); the Pampas and Brazilian city lawns.
animal.season: Resident in Florida and southward; northern Great Plains birds are summer visitors, Apr–Oct

lore: Its species name cunicularia, 'little miner' or 'burrower', was given by Juan Ignacio Molina in Chile in 1782.
funFact: Though globally common, it is listed as Endangered in Canada after its prairie populations collapsed.

summary: A large, round-headed owl of eastern swamps and forests with soulful dark eyes and a call that asks 'Who cooks for you?'. In the last century it spread across Canada into the Pacific Northwest, where it now outcompetes the threatened Spotted Owl.
nativeRange: Eastern North America and central Mexico; expanded across boreal Canada into British Columbia, Washington, Oregon and northern California during the 20th century
abilities: Calls frequently by day as well as night
Takes a wide range of prey including crayfish, fish and frogs
Its westward range expansion is one of the largest documented for a North American bird

animal.diet: Small mammals, birds, amphibians, crayfish, fish, insects
animal.habitat: Mature forest near water — swamps, river bottoms, old woodlots
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform raucous 'caterwauling' duets of hoots, cackles and screams.
fieldMarks: Large, round head without ear tufts
Dark brown eyes
Horizontal barring on upper breast, vertical streaks on the belly
Grey-brown plumage with a yellow bill
animal.voice: A rhythmic hooting 'who cooks for you, who cooks for you-all', ending in a drawl; also monkey-like cackles.
animal.lookalikes: Spotted Owl (West) is darker with white spots instead of bars and streaks. Great Gray Owl is larger with yellow eyes. Great Horned Owl has ear tufts and yellow eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Southern swamps such as Corkscrew Swamp and the Okefenokee, river bottomlands across the east, and forests of the Pacific Northwest.

lore: Its spread into the range of the Northern Spotted Owl led the US Fish and Wildlife Service to adopt a 2024 management plan that includes culling Barred Owls in parts of the Pacific Northwest.
funFact: Barred Owls sometimes wade into shallow water to catch fish and crayfish.

summary: A gaudily patterned duck that nests in tree holes, sometimes many metres up. A day after hatching, the ducklings leap to the ground without opening their wings and walk to water.
nativeRange: Eastern North America, the Pacific coast from British Columbia to California, and Cuba
abilities: Nests in tree cavities and nest boxes, often in old Pileated Woodpecker holes
Ducklings jump from cavities up to about 15 m high without injury
Claws on its feet let it perch on branches
Females often lay eggs in each other's nests ('egg dumping')

animal.diet: Acorns, seeds, aquatic plants, insects
animal.habitat: Wooded swamps, beaver ponds, slow rivers and marshes with trees
animal.behaviour: It flies nimbly through flooded forest, often nodding its head in flight.
fieldMarks: Male: iridescent green-and-purple crested head with white chin straps and red eye
Male: chestnut breast flecked white, buff sides, black-and-white bar on shoulder
Female: grey-brown with a white teardrop-shaped eye-ring and a short crest
Long, broad tail and short neck in flight
animal.voice: Female gives a loud, squealing, rising 'oo-eek!' when flushed; male a thin, rising whistle 'jeeeb'.
animal.lookalikes: Mandarin Duck (escaped from collections) has orange 'sails' on the back and whiskery orange cheeks. Hooded Merganser has a thin bill and a fan-shaped white or brown crest.
animal.whereToSee: Wooded swamps and park ponds across the eastern US, e.g. the Great Swamp NWR (New Jersey) and Okefenokee; nest-box programmes on many refuges.
animal.season: Resident in the southern US; summer visitor in the north, Mar–Nov

lore: Hunted almost to extinction by about 1900, it recovered after the 1918 Migratory Bird Treaty Act ended market hunting and nest-box programmes replaced lost tree cavities; Catesby painted it as 'The Summer Duck'.
funFact: Linnaeus named it sponsa, Latin for 'betrothed' or 'bride', for the male's 'wedding finery'.

summary: A tall grey crane with a red crown whose rolling, bugling calls carry for kilometres. Each spring hundreds of thousands gather on Nebraska's Platte River, one of North America's great wildlife spectacles.
nativeRange: Breeds across Alaska, Canada, the northern US and north-eastern Siberia; resident populations in Florida, Mississippi and Cuba; winters in the southern US and northern Mexico
abilities: Its windpipe coils into the breastbone, producing calls audible several kilometres away
Pairs perform leaping, bowing courtship dances and 'unison calls'
Paints its grey feathers rusty-brown by preening with iron-rich mud
Migrates in high, circling flocks riding thermals

animal.diet: Waste grain, tubers, seeds, insects, snails, small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Marshes, wet meadows, tundra and farm fields near shallow roosting water
animal.behaviour: Families stay together through the first winter, with colts learning migration routes from their parents.
fieldMarks: Tall grey crane with long neck and legs
Red bare forecrown and white cheeks
Bushy 'bustle' of tertial feathers over the tail
Flies with neck fully outstretched; often stained rusty brown
animal.voice: A loud, rolling, trumpeting rattle 'garoo-oo-oo'; juveniles give high, whistling 'peeps'.
animal.lookalikes: Great Blue Heron flies with its neck folded and lacks the red crown. Whooping Crane is white with black wingtips. Common Crane (rare vagrant) has a black-and-white neck.
animal.whereToSee: Platte River near Kearney, Nebraska (Feb–Apr, Rowe Sanctuary); Bosque del Apache NWR (New Mexico) and Whitewater Draw (Arizona) in winter; Jasper-Pulaski (Indiana) in autumn.
animal.season: Migratory populations: on the Platte mid-Feb–early Apr; on wintering grounds Nov–Feb

lore: Aldo Leopold's essay 'Marshland Elegy' in A Sand County Almanac (1949) made the sandhill crane a symbol of wildness and deep time; in Ojibwe tradition the crane (ajijaak) is a leading clan.
funFact: Its rusty colour is not pigment at all but mud painted on during preening.

summary: The tallest bird in North America, a white crane whose only migratory flock fell to about 15 birds in 1941. Protection of its only wild migratory flock, which nests in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park and winters on the Texas coast, has brought it back to several hundred.
nativeRange: Wild flock breeds in Wood Buffalo National Park (Alberta/Northwest Territories) and winters at Aransas, Texas; reintroduced non-migratory birds in Louisiana and an eastern migratory flock in Wisconsin
abilities: Migrates about 4,000 km between Canada and the Gulf of Mexico
Windpipe up to about 1.5 m long, coiled in the breastbone, amplifying its bugle
Pairs bond for life and defend large winter territories in salt marsh
Captive-raised cranes have been taught migration routes by following ultralight aircraft (2001–2015)

animal.diet: Blue crabs, clams, wolfberries and acorns in winter; insects, frogs, fish and plants in summer
animal.habitat: Remote boreal marshes for breeding; coastal salt marshes and bays in winter
animal.size: About 1.5 m tall; wingspan 2–2.3 m; 4.5–8.5 kg
animal.behaviour: Pairs usually lay two eggs but often raise only one chick.
fieldMarks: Snow-white body and very tall stature
Black primary feathers visible as black wingtips in flight
Red crown and black 'moustache' on the face
Juveniles mottled cinnamon and white
animal.voice: A loud, clear, trumpeting 'whoop-whoop' unison call that carries several kilometres.
animal.lookalikes: American White Pelican has black on the whole outer wing and a huge bill. Wood Stork has a dark bare head and black trailing wing edges. Great Egret flies with neck folded. Sandhill Crane is grey.
animal.whereToSee: Aransas National Wildlife Refuge and boat tours from Rockport–Fulton, Texas (Nov–Mar); Necedah NWR, Wisconsin (eastern flock).
animal.season: Winter at Aransas Nov–Mar; breeding in Wood Buffalo May–Sep

lore: Its nesting grounds were not found until 1954, when a forest-fire crew spotted cranes in Wood Buffalo National Park; it was among the first species listed as endangered in the United States, in 1967.
