funFact: The US Fish and Wildlife Service estimated about 540 whooping cranes wintered in and around Aransas in 2025–26, up from roughly 15 in 1941.

summary: The largest heron in North America, a patient, statuesque hunter of marshes, lakes and coasts. It strikes fish with a lightning thrust of its dagger bill and swallows them whole.
nativeRange: Alaska and southern Canada through the US and Mexico to Central America, the West Indies and northern South America; also the Galápagos
abilities: Specialised neck vertebrae allow a sudden, spring-loaded strike
Hunts by day and night, aided by many rod cells in its eyes
Nests colonially in heronries that can hold hundreds of nests high in trees
Swallows prey up to large fish, rodents and even small birds

animal.diet: Fish, frogs, crayfish, rodents, snakes, insects
animal.habitat: Almost any shallow fresh or salt water
animal.behaviour: An all-white form, the 'Great White Heron', lives in the Florida Keys and Caribbean.
fieldMarks: Tall, blue-grey heron with a long neck and dagger-like yellow bill
White face with a black stripe extending into head plumes
Rufous thighs and edge of the wing
Flies with slow wingbeats, neck folded in an S, legs trailing
animal.voice: A deep, harsh croak 'frahnk' when disturbed; bill-clattering at colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Sandhill Crane flies with neck outstretched and has a red crown. Grey Heron (Eurasia) lacks rufous thighs. Little Blue Heron is much smaller and darker. White form vs Great Egret: Great Egret has black legs and is slimmer.
animal.whereToSee: Wetlands throughout North America — e.g. the Everglades, Chesapeake Bay, San Francisco Bay, Pacific Northwest heronries.
animal.season: Resident in much of the US; northern birds migrate south in winter

funFact: Despite standing over a metre tall, it typically weighs only about 2–2.5 kg, thanks to hollow bones.

summary: A bright pink wader with a flat, spoon-shaped bill that it sweeps side to side through shallow water to feel for prey. Its colour comes from carotenoid pigments in the crustaceans it eats.
nativeRange: Gulf coasts of the US (Florida, Louisiana, Texas), the Caribbean, and Central and South America to Argentina
abilities: Catches prey by touch: nerve endings in the bill snap it shut on contact
Turns pink from canthaxanthin and other carotenoids in shrimp and crabs
Nests colonially in mangroves and trees with herons and ibises

animal.diet: Small fish, shrimp, crayfish, aquatic insects
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal and freshwater wetlands, mangroves and mudflats
animal.behaviour: Feeding groups wade in lines, sweeping their bills in unison.
fieldMarks: Pink body, deeper red on the shoulders and rump
Long, flat bill widening into a spatulate 'spoon'
Bare greenish head in adults
Orange tail and red legs; flies with neck outstretched
animal.voice: Mostly silent; low grunts and croaks at nesting colonies.
animal.lookalikes: American Flamingo has a very long neck and a bent, downturned bill. Scarlet Ibis is uniformly scarlet with a decurved bill.
animal.whereToSee: J. N. 'Ding' Darling NWR (Sanibel, Florida), the Everglades, the Texas coast, the Pantanal and the Venezuelan Llanos.
animal.season: Resident in Florida and the tropics; post-breeding wanderers move north in summer

lore: In the 19th century spoonbill wings were sold in Florida as fans, and plume hunting nearly wiped out the US population before protections such as the 1918 Migratory Bird Treaty Act.
funFact: The name ajaja is from a Tupi–Guaraní name for the bird, recorded by early naturalists in Brazil.

summary: An intensely scarlet ibis of South American mangroves and mudflats whose colour comes from carotenoids in its crab and shrimp diet. At dusk, flocks returning to roost in Trinidad's Caroni Swamp turn the mangroves red.
nativeRange: Northern coasts of South America from Colombia and Venezuela through the Guianas to north-eastern Brazil; Trinidad and Tobago
abilities: Probes mud with a long decurved bill to find crabs and molluscs by touch
Gathers in roosts of thousands in mangrove islands
Hybridises with the American White Ibis where they meet in Venezuela

animal.diet: Crabs, shrimp, molluscs, insects and small fish
animal.habitat: Mangroves, tidal mudflats, estuaries and flooded savanna
animal.behaviour: Young birds are grey-brown and white and gradually turn scarlet over their first two years.
fieldMarks: Entirely scarlet plumage
Black tips to the outer primaries
Long, decurved, dark-reddish bill
Flies with neck outstretched in lines or V-formations
animal.voice: Generally quiet; hoarse, nasal honks and grunts in flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Roseate Spoonbill is pink with a flat spoon bill. American Flamingo is far larger with a long neck. White Ibis is white with black wingtips.
animal.whereToSee: Caroni Swamp, Trinidad (dusk boat tours); the Venezuelan Llanos; coastal Amapá and Maranhão, Brazil.

lore: The Tupinambá of coastal Brazil made ceremonial feather mantles from guará plumes; one held in Copenhagen's National Museum since the 17th century was returned to Brazil in 2024. It is the national bird of Trinidad and Tobago.
funFact: Captive scarlet ibises fade to pink unless their food contains carotenoids.

summary: A medium-sized penguin of the desert coasts of Peru and Chile, living on the cold, fish-rich Humboldt Current. It once nested in burrows dug into guano deposits metres deep, until 19th-century guano mining stripped them away.
nativeRange: Pacific coasts and offshore islands of Peru and Chile
abilities: Thrives on a hot desert coast thanks to bare facial skin that sheds heat
Dives repeatedly to catch anchovies and sardines in cold upwelling water
Nests in burrows, caves and crevices to protect eggs from sun

animal.diet: Anchoveta, sardines, other small fish and squid
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts and islands near the Humboldt Current
animal.lifespan: About 15–20 years in the wild; over 30 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Breeding often fails in strong El Niño years, when warm water drives fish away.
fieldMarks: Black back and white front with a single broad black band across the breast
White C-shaped band from the eye around the cheeks to the throat
Pink bare skin at the base of the black bill
Black spots scattered on the white belly
animal.voice: Loud, donkey-like braying calls at colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Magellanic Penguin (overlaps in central Chile) has two black breast bands. Galápagos Penguin is smaller with a thinner face stripe and lives only on the Galápagos.
animal.whereToSee: Islas Ballestas (Paracas, Peru), Punta San Juan (Peru), and the Humboldt Penguin National Reserve with Isla Damas and Isla Choros (Chile).

lore: It is named after Alexander von Humboldt, whose name also labels the cold ocean current on which it depends; the guano it nests in was exported as fertiliser in the Peruvian 'Guano Age' of the mid-1800s.
funFact: Its Spanish nickname 'pájaro niño', 'child bird', comes from its upright, toddling walk.

summary: A heavy, dagger-billed diving bird of northern lakes whose wailing and yodelling calls are the signature sound of the North Woods. Its legs are set so far back that it can barely walk on land.
nativeRange: Breeds across Alaska, Canada, the northern US, Greenland and Iceland; winters on Atlantic and Pacific coasts of North America and western Europe
abilities: Dives to about 60 m and stays under for up to a minute or more
Has dense, mostly solid bones that reduce buoyancy
Needs a runway of 30 m to several hundred metres of water to take off
Each male has a distinctive yodel that changes if he moves to a new territory

animal.diet: Fish such as perch and suckers; crayfish and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Clear northern lakes with fish and islands for nesting; ocean bays in winter
animal.behaviour: Chicks ride on their parents' backs for their first weeks.
fieldMarks: Breeding: black head with green gloss, red eye and dagger-like black bill
Breeding: white-striped necklace and checkerboard black-and-white back
Winter: grey-brown above, white throat, pale bill
Sits low in the water; in flight shows hunched back and feet trailing past the tail
animal.voice: A haunting wail, a quavering tremolo ('crazy laughter'), the male's rising yodel, and a soft hoot.
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-billed Loon has a pale, upturned bill. Pacific Loon is smaller with a grey nape and rounded head. Double-crested Cormorant has a hooked bill and swims with head tilted up.
animal.whereToSee: Lakes of Minnesota (Boundary Waters), Maine, the Adirondacks, Ontario's Algonquin Park; Atlantic and Pacific coasts in winter.
animal.season: On breeding lakes Apr–Oct; on coasts Nov–Apr

lore: Canada's one-dollar coin, introduced in 1987, carries a loon and is universally called the 'loonie'; in Ojibwe tradition the loon (maang) is a leadership clan, and it is Minnesota's state bird.
funFact: Loons have been shown to change their yodel when they move territories, apparently to sound unlike the previous owner.

summary: A small, sand-coloured plover that nests on open beaches and lakeshores, where its eggs are almost invisible. Beach development and disturbance made it a flagship of shorebird conservation, with nests now fenced and patrolled across its range.
nativeRange: Breeds on the Atlantic coast from Newfoundland to North Carolina, around the Great Lakes, and on the northern Great Plains; winters on the south Atlantic and Gulf coasts, the Bahamas, the Caribbean and Mexico
abilities: Eggs and chicks are camouflaged against pale sand
Adults perform broken-wing displays to lure predators from nests
Chicks feed themselves within hours of hatching
Foot-trembles on wet sand to startle invertebrates

animal.diet: Marine worms, insects, small crustaceans and molluscs
animal.habitat: Open sandy beaches, sandbars and alkali flats with sparse vegetation
animal.behaviour: It runs in short bursts and stops abruptly, typical of plovers.
fieldMarks: Pale, dry-sand upperparts — paler than any other North American ringed plover
Bright orange legs
Breeding: short orange bill with a black tip, single black breast band and black forehead bar
Winter: bill all dark, breast band faint or partial
animal.voice: A soft, clear, whistled 'peep-lo' or 'peep', like a piped note.
animal.lookalikes: Semipalmated Plover has a dark mud-brown back. Snowy Plover has dark legs and a thin black bill. Wilson's Plover has a heavy black bill and pinkish legs.
animal.whereToSee: Cape Cod and Long Island beaches, Sleeping Bear Dunes (Michigan), Chicago's Montrose Beach, and Gulf coast beaches of Texas and Florida in winter.
animal.season: Breeding grounds Apr–Aug; winter coasts Aug–Apr

lore: Two Great Lakes piping plovers named Monty and Rose nested on Chicago's Montrose Beach from 2019, the first in the city in decades, and became local celebrities.
funFact: The Great Lakes population fell to fewer than 20 pairs in the 1980s before intensive protection helped it grow again.

summary: The most vividly coloured flamingo, a deep coral-pink bird that filters shrimp and algae from salty lagoons with its head upside-down. It is the national bird of the Bahamas.
nativeRange: The Caribbean (Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, Bonaire), Yucatán Peninsula, northern coast of South America and the Galápagos; increasingly seen in Florida
abilities: Filter-feeds with a bent bill held upside-down, pumping water through comb-like lamellae with its tongue
Gets its colour from carotenoid pigments in brine shrimp and algae
Stands on one leg with little or no muscular effort, using passive locking of the joints
Builds mud-mound nests in dense colonies

animal.diet: Brine shrimp, small molluscs, insect larvae, algae and seeds
animal.habitat: Shallow saline and brackish lagoons, salt pans and estuaries
animal.behaviour: Flocks perform synchronised 'marching' displays — head-flagging and wing salutes — that stimulate breeding.
fieldMarks: Deep pink-orange body, brighter than other flamingos
Pale pink bill with the outer third black, sharply bent downward
Very long pink legs and neck
In flight, black flight feathers contrast with pink-red wing coverts
animal.voice: Goose-like honking, given constantly in flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Greater Flamingo (Old World) is paler pink with a pink bill with less black. Chilean Flamingo has grey legs with pink 'knees'. Roseate Spoonbill has a flat bill and short neck.
animal.whereToSee: Inagua National Park (Bahamas), Ría Celestún and Ría Lagartos (Yucatán), Bonaire's salt pans, Galápagos lagoons; Florida Bay and the Everglades.
animal.season: Resident year-round; Yucatán flocks largest Nov–Mar at Celestún

lore: John James Audubon's life-size plate of the American Flamingo, bent to fit the page, is one of the best-known images in The Birds of America (1827–38); Mark Catesby painted it a century earlier in the Bahamas.
funFact: After Hurricane Idalia in 2023, dozens of American flamingos were blown north and seen across Florida and as far north as Ohio and Wisconsin.

summary: The largest flying parrot by length, about a metre from bill to tail, in deep cobalt blue. Its bill cracks palm nuts too hard for almost any other animal, and it was trapped heavily for the pet trade in the 1980s.
nativeRange: Pantanal of Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay; the Cerrado of interior Brazil; and parts of eastern Amazonia (Pará)
abilities: Cracks extremely hard palm nuts, chiefly acuri (Attalea phalerata) and bocaiúva (Acrocomia aculeata)
Picks palm nuts out of cattle dung, after the cattle have digested the pulp
Uses a 'file' — ridges inside the upper bill — to grip nuts while cracking
Depends on large tree cavities, especially in the manduvi tree (Sterculia apetala), for nesting

animal.diet: Palm nuts almost exclusively; some fruit
animal.habitat: Open palm savanna and wooded wetlands with large nesting trees
animal.behaviour: Nest boxes and protected nest trees in the Pantanal, through the Instituto Arara Azul led by Neiva Guedes since 1990, have helped the population recover.
fieldMarks: Entirely cobalt-blue plumage
Bright yellow eye-ring and yellow crescent of bare skin at the base of the lower mandible
Huge, dark grey-black hooked bill
Very long, tapering tail
animal.voice: Deep, rasping, guttural screeches 'graaa-aah', audible from far away.
animal.lookalikes: Lear's Macaw (north-eastern Bahia only) is smaller, with a greenish tinge and a larger, paler yellow facial patch. Glaucous Macaw, paler and greyer, is probably extinct.
animal.whereToSee: The Pantanal of Mato Grosso do Sul and Mato Grosso, e.g. Refúgio Ecológico Caiman and lodges along the Transpantaneira.

lore: In the 1980s an estimated 10,000 hyacinth macaws were taken from the wild for the pet trade; it is now listed on CITES Appendix I.
funFact: In the Pantanal about 90% of its nests are in manduvi trees — and the Toco Toucan, which spreads manduvi seeds, is also one of its main egg predators.

summary: Puerto Rico's only surviving native parrot, a green amazon with a red forehead that fell to just 13 wild birds in 1975. Captive breeding and releases have kept it alive, though hurricanes repeatedly set back the wild flocks.
nativeRange: Endemic to Puerto Rico (formerly also Culebra and Vieques); wild populations now in El Yunque, Río Abajo and Maricao
abilities: Nests in deep natural tree cavities, especially in old palo colorado trees
Gives loud flight calls that keep pairs and flocks in contact over forest
Feeds on more than 50 kinds of native fruits, seeds and flowers

animal.diet: Fruits, seeds, flowers and leaves of native forest trees
animal.habitat: Humid upland forest and limestone karst forest
animal.behaviour: Pairs stay together year-round and fly side by side, wings almost touching.
fieldMarks: Bright green plumage with darker scaling
Narrow red band across the forehead
Broad white eye-ring
Vivid blue primaries visible in flight
animal.voice: A loud, bugling squawk; its Taíno name iguaca imitates the call.
animal.lookalikes: Hispaniolan Amazon (introduced and established in Puerto Rico) is larger, with a white forehead and a maroon belly patch. Escaped pet parrots also occur in San Juan.
animal.whereToSee: Río Abajo State Forest near Arecibo and El Yunque National Forest; the Iguaca Aviary and Río Abajo aviary run breeding programmes.

lore: Columbus's expeditions found abundant parrots on Puerto Rico, where the Taíno called them iguaca; deforestation reduced a population once estimated at around a million to a handful by the 1970s.
funFact: Hurricane Maria in 2017 wiped out most of the wild El Yunque flock, but birds in the Río Abajo population largely survived.

summary: Cuba's national bird, whose red belly, white chest and blue crown echo the colours of the Cuban flag. Its name tocororo imitates its repeated call.
nativeRange: Endemic to Cuba, including Isla de la Juventud
abilities: Sallies from a perch to pluck fruit and insects in hovering flight
Nests in old woodpecker holes and natural cavities
Unusual among trogons for its notched, ragged-edged tail feathers

animal.diet: Flowers, fruit and insects
animal.habitat: Shady forest of all types, from lowlands to mountains
animal.behaviour: Like other trogons it sits motionless for long periods, making it easy to overlook until it calls.
fieldMarks: Blue-violet crown and bright green back
White throat and breast; bright red belly
Long tail with uniquely notched, flared feather tips; white spotting beneath
Wings barred black and white
animal.voice: A repeated, hollow 'to-co-ro, to-co-ro', and a low 'cucuu'.
animal.lookalikes: No other trogon occurs in Cuba; Hispaniolan Trogon lives only on Hispaniola.
animal.whereToSee: Zapata Swamp (Ciénaga de Zapata), Viñales, Topes de Collantes and the Sierra Maestra.

lore: Cuban tradition holds that the tocororo cannot survive in a cage — a symbol of a people's love of liberty, which helped make it the national bird.
funFact: Its genus name Priotelus comes from Greek for 'saw' and 'end', for the jagged tips of its tail feathers.

summary: A colourful motmot with a long tail ending in two bare-shafted 'rackets' that it swings like a pendulum. It is the national bird of both El Salvador and Nicaragua.
nativeRange: South-eastern Mexico (including the Yucatán Peninsula) through Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua to north-western Costa Rica
abilities: Its tail rackets form when weakly attached barbs near the tips fall off during preening and wear
Wags its tail in a pendulum display aimed at predators — a signal that it has seen them
Digs long nesting tunnels in earth banks, quarries, wells and Maya ruins

animal.diet: Large insects, spiders, small lizards and frogs; some fruit
animal.habitat: Open dry forest, edges, gardens, riverbanks and cenotes
animal.behaviour: It often nests colonially in the walls of Yucatán cenotes and limestone sinkholes.
fieldMarks: Long tail with bare shafts ending in blue-and-black rackets
Bright turquoise eyebrow stripe above a black mask
Black throat stripe edged with turquoise
Rufous back and belly; blue-green wings
animal.voice: A low, hollow, croaking 'kwaa' or 'cowak', often at dawn.
animal.lookalikes: Lesson's Motmot has a blue crown ring around a black cap and a green body. Russet-crowned Motmot has a rufous crown.
animal.whereToSee: Cenotes and Maya sites of the Yucatán such as Ek Balam and Cobá, Guanacaste (Costa Rica), and dry forests of El Salvador and Nicaragua.

lore: El Salvador's torogoz and Nicaragua's guardabarranco ('ravine guardian') are both this species; its pendulum-like tail earned it the Yucatán name pájaro reloj, 'clock bird'.
funFact: It is a 'pursuit-deterrent' signaller: tail-wagging tells predators they have been spotted and a chase is pointless.

summary: North America's largest gamebird and the wild ancestor of the domestic turkey, first domesticated in Mesoamerica over 2,000 years ago. Hunted to near-extinction by the early 1900s, it now numbers in the millions.
nativeRange: Much of the United States, southern Canada and northern Mexico; introduced elsewhere, including Hawaii and New Zealand
abilities: Domesticated independently in Mesoamerica and by Ancestral Puebloans in the American Southwest
Can burst into flight and roosts high in trees at night
Males gobble to attract females; calls carry over a kilometre
Bare head and neck change colour from red to white and blue with excitement

animal.diet: Acorns, nuts, seeds, berries, insects and small reptiles
animal.habitat: Mixed forest with clearings, oak woods, farm edges, and increasingly suburbs
animal.lifespan: Usually 3–5 years in the wild; records over 13
animal.size: Males 100–125 cm and 5–11 kg; females much smaller
animal.behaviour: Males strut in spring with tails fanned, wings dragged and feathers puffed.
fieldMarks: Very large, dark, iridescent bronze-green plumage
Bare blue-and-red head with a fleshy snood over the bill and wattles at the throat
Males carry a hair-like 'beard' on the breast and leg spurs
Tail tipped rusty or buff (varies by subspecies), fanned in display
animal.voice: Males' rolling gobble; also yelps, clucks, purrs and a sharp 'putt' alarm.
animal.lookalikes: Ocellated Turkey (Yucatán) has a blue head with orange knobs and eyespots on the tail. Domestic turkeys are usually white or patchy and heavier.
animal.whereToSee: Open woods and field edges across the eastern US; often seen in suburbs and along rural roads.

lore: In a 1784 letter to his daughter, Benjamin Franklin called the Bald Eagle 'a Bird of bad moral Character' and the turkey 'a much more respectable Bird'; for the Aztecs turkeys were important ritual and food animals, associated with the god Tezcatlipoca in the form Chalchiuhtotolin.
funFact: Europeans called it 'turkey' because they confused it with guineafowl imported through Turkish lands.

summary: The largest bird in the Americas, a flightless ratite of the pampas and savannas of South America. Males alone build the nest, incubate eggs laid by several females, and fiercely guard the chicks.
nativeRange: Eastern and central South America: Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina; a feral population in northern Germany descends from escaped birds
abilities: Runs at up to about 60 km/h, using its wings like rudders to zigzag
One male's nest may hold dozens of eggs laid by several females
Males defend chicks aggressively, charging people and horses
Eats plants toxic or unpalatable to many grazers

animal.diet: Broad-leaved plants, seeds, fruit, insects, small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Open grassland, savanna and farmland
animal.lifespan: Around 10–15 years in the wild; longer in captivity
animal.size: Up to about 1.5 m tall; 20–40 kg
animal.behaviour: Outside the breeding season rheas form flocks of 10–100, often alongside deer, guanacos or cattle.
fieldMarks: Very large, flightless, grey-brown bird with a long neck
Black feathering at the base of the neck and upper back in males
Three forward-pointing toes
Shaggy, drooping wings covering the body
animal.voice: Breeding males give a deep, booming 'nan-doo'.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser (Darwin's) Rhea of Patagonia and the high Andes is smaller and spotted white. There are no other large flightless birds in South America.
animal.whereToSee: The Pampas of Argentina and Uruguay, Emas National Park and the Pantanal (Brazil), the Chaco of Paraguay.

lore: Guaraní and other Indigenous peoples of Brazil see a rhea constellation (Ema) in the sky near the Southern Cross; gauchos hunted it on horseback with boleadoras.
funFact: Its genus name Rhea comes from the mother of the gods in Greek myth.
